title: Knowing and choosing (5:5)
hookLine: how can God know and we still choose? God's knowing isn't like ours
tomorrow: can a door close so long it won't open again?

lines: THE NEXT SHOW, ALREADY LINED UP.
cards: The streaming app has the next show lined up before this one ends, and it's annoyingly right. A best friend orders for you at the counter, and gets it exactly. Being known that well can feel cozy, or a little cornering.
Now scale it all the way up. If God knows what I'll choose, am I still choosing? One question for today, and Maimonides asks it in his own words before anyone else can.

teach.h: IF GOD KNOWS, CAN I CHOOSE?
teach.b: You might ask, he writes: doesn't God know everything before it happens? Then either God knows this person will be righteous, and they can't be otherwise, or they can, and God didn't know.
His first answer is honesty: the answer is longer than the earth and wider than the sea. Then the core. People know with a knowledge that's separate from themselves; we and our knowing are two.

teach.h: GOD AND GOD'S KNOWING ARE ONE.
teach.b: God and God's knowing are one, and a human mind can't grasp that, just as it can't grasp God. He quotes Isaiah: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways." So we don't know how God knows.
But we know without doubt that a person's deeds are in their own hands. Now a neighbor.

Boethius, a Christian philosopher, wrote in his Consolation of Philosophy that God sees from an eternal present, and that seeing someone walk doesn't make them walk. What the two share: neither gives up either side.
God knows, and we choose, and God's knowing isn't like ours.
The honest difference: Boethius offers a picture to help the mind hold it. Maimonides stops on purpose, because any picture would make God's knowing too much like ours.
For him, the answer stays beyond our knowing.

how: The puzzle of God's knowledge and human choice is studied in Jewish philosophy alongside Pirkei Avot's saying that all is foreseen, yet freedom is given; Maimonides' answer in Hilkhot Teshuvah 5:5 is a classic text for it.

o: God learns our choices only after we make them
God plans each choice, and we follow the script
God knows our choices, yet we still truly choose

games.q: two answers to one puzzle — tap the pairs.
p: one with God, beyond our grasp
my thoughts are not your thoughts
God sees from an eternal present

s: if God knows your choice ahead of time, you aren't really choosing
Maimonides: we don't know how God knows, but we know without doubt our deeds are in our hands.
Maimonides admits the answer is longer than the earth and wider than the sea
he opens his answer by saying how big the question is.
Maimonides and Boethius explain the puzzle the same way
both keep God's knowing and human choice; Boethius offers a picture, Maimonides says it's beyond us.

games.q: your study partner says: 'if God already knows how I'll do on the exam, why study?' which reply fits Maimonides?
o: God knows, and you still choose; how both are true is beyond us. so study.
God doesn't know the future, so the result really is all up to you.
it's already known, so the outcome is settled; studying won't change it.
games.why: Maimonides keeps both: God's knowing, which isn't like ours, and a person's deeds, which are in their own hands.

practice: Close your eyes and hold two sentences side by side, without forcing them to agree: I am known. I am choosing. When the mind tries to solve it, let it rest, and keep both in view until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Knowing and choosing: Maimonides' answer to the old puzzle. God knows, a person chooses, and how both are true lies beyond our knowing.

orig.note: Hebrew: choice, free will; Maimonides' chapter five is about it.

carryVoice: For the road: beyond our knowing, and still, your deeds are in your hands. Day fifteen fifty-three, held.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 5:5 (God's foreknowledge and human choice; God and God's knowledge are one; deeds are in a person's hands)
